Lucretius sets out Epicurus's physics: everything that exists is made of atoms, too small to be seen, moving through the void. As they fall, they sometimes swerve a little, the clinamen, and these collisions form things, living beings, worlds. The soul itself is made of atoms and dissolves at death: so there is nothing to fear. He also describes the birth of species, lightning, earthquakes and the plague of Athens.

He describes everything: prospecting for veins, digging galleries, pumping water, ventilation, crushing and washing ore, smelting, refining gold and silver. He also discusses dangers and accidents. The two hundred ninety-two woodcuts show the machines in such detail that they could be rebuilt. The book remained the mining manual for a hundred and eighty years.

textes.Lavoisier veut faire de la chimie une sc: Lavoisier wants to make chemistry as rigorous a science as physics. His rule: weigh everything, before and after each reaction. He thus shows that total mass is conserved, even when gas escapes. He explains combustion and respiration by oxygen, and abandons “phlogiston,” the imaginary fluid that bodies were supposed to lose when burning. He draws up a list of 33 simple substances, the ancestors of our elements, even if light and caloric are still on it. Finally, he imposes a new nomenclature: “copper sulfate” rather than “blue vitriol.”

With a simple candle, he explains almost all the chemistry and physics of his time. Why does the flame have this shape? Where does the wax go? He shows that the candle produces water and carbon dioxide, that the air contains the oxygen needed for combustion, and that we too “burn” our food when we breathe. Every experiment is done before the audience's eyes. It is one of the first great classics of popular science.

He shows that carbon forms four bonds and can link to itself in long chains, which explains the immense variety of the molecules of life. In 1865, he proposes a ring structure of six carbon atoms for benzene. He draws his molecules with elongated shapes, known as “Kekulé sausages,” before simple lines took over. With these rules, chemists can at last explain how many different molecules exist for the same formula.

That is what allows salt water to conduct current. From this he drew a simple definition of acids, which release hydrogen ions, and bases, which release hydroxide ions. She describes radiation, how to measure it, the radioactive elements, including the polonium and radium she discovered with Pierre Curie, and the transformation of one element into another. He explains how electrons are shared between atoms, why some bonds are stronger, why molecules have precise shapes. He invents the electronegativity scale, which measures how greedy an atom is for electrons, and the idea of resonance for molecules like benzene. The book became the reference textbook for a whole generation of chemists. Pauling then turned to the great molecules of life and discovered the alpha helix of proteins.

textes.Rachel Carson, biologiste marine, enquêt: Rachel Carson, a marine biologist, investigates synthetic pesticides like DDT, spread massively after the war. She shows that they don't only kill the targeted insects: they accumulate along the food chain, concentrate in fish and birds, and impair their reproduction. Hence the image of a spring without birdsong. She also documents the risks to human health, and the emergence of resistant insects. The chemical industry attacked her fiercely. But the book triggered a presidential inquiry, then the ban on DDT for agriculture in the United States in 1972.

textes.Son nom vient du grec « paresseux » : il: Its name comes from the Greek for “lazy”: it reacts with almost nothing. Yet it makes up nearly 1% of the air.
textes.Son symbole K vient du latin kalium. Dav: Its symbol K comes from the Latin kalium. Davy isolated it in 1807, a few days before sodium.
textes.Le corps humain en contient environ un k: The human body contains about a kilogram of it, almost all in the skeleton.
textes.Une des cases vides de Mendeleïev, qu'il: One of Mendeleev's empty squares, which he called “eka-boron.” Nilson discovered it in 1879.
textes.L'essentiel du titane extrait finit en b: Most of the titanium mined ends up as titanium white, a very opaque pigment: paint, paper, sunscreen.
textes.Henry Ford utilisait de l'acier au vanad: Henry Ford used vanadium steel in the Model T, lighter and stronger.
textes.Son nom vient du grec « couleur » : ses: Its name comes from the Greek for “color”: its compounds are green, yellow, orange. The ruby owes it its red.
textes.Les artistes de la préhistoire ont peint: Prehistoric artists painted caves with manganese black, tens of thousands of years ago.
textes.Le noyau terrestre est surtout fait de f: The Earth's core is mostly iron. Beyond iron, fusion no longer yields energy: when the core of a big star is full of it, the star collapses.
textes.Les mineurs allemands accusaient le kobo: German miners blamed the kobold, a goblin, for spoiling their ore. Cobalt kept the name.
textes.Encore un lutin : Kupfernickel, « le cui: Another goblin: Kupfernickel, “the devil's copper,” the ore that looked like copper without yielding any.
textes.La statue de la Liberté était couleur cu: The Statue of Liberty was copper-colored when it arrived. Verdigris covered it in about twenty years.
textes.Les toits gris de Paris sont en zinc, po: The gray rooftops of Paris are zinc, laid en masse during Haussmann's works.
textes.la cuillère qui fond dans le thé: the spoon that melts in tea
textes.Il fond à 30 °C, donc dans la main. Mend: It melts at 30 °C, so in your hand. Mendeleev had predicted its mass and density under the name eka-aluminum.
textes.Encore une prédiction de Mendeleïev, l'é: Another of Mendeleev's predictions, eka-silicon. Winkler found it in 1886 and named it after Germany.
textes.La « poudre de succession » des empoison: Poisoners' “inheritance powder.” The Marsh test, in 1836, made it possible to detect it in corpses.
textes.Une ou deux noix du Brésil suffisent à c: One or two Brazil nuts are enough to cover the daily need for selenium. A handful is too much.
textes.Un des deux seuls éléments liquides à te: One of only two elements that are liquid at room temperature, with mercury. Its name means “stench.”
textes.De 1960 à 1983, le mètre était défini pa: From 1960 to 1983, the meter was defined by an orange line of krypton-86.
textes.les horloges atomiques des satellites GP: the atomic clocks of GPS satellites
textes.Il s'enflamme spontanément à l'air. Les: It ignites spontaneously in air. Rubidium clocks keep time aboard GPS satellites.
textes.Nommé d'après Strontian, un village écos: Named after Strontian, a Scottish village. The red in fireworks is strontium.
textes.Ytterby, une carrière suédoise, a donné: Ytterby, a Swedish quarry, gave its name to four elements: yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium.
textes.La zircone cubique brille plus que le di: Cubic zirconia sparkles more than diamond, but it is less hard and weighs almost twice as much for the same size.
textes.Les aimants supraconducteurs du LHC et d: The superconducting magnets of the LHC and of MRI scanners are wound with niobium-titanium wire.
textes.Les bactéries qui fixent l'azote de l'ai: The bacteria that fix nitrogen from the air need a molybdenum enzyme.
textes.Le premier élément fabriqué par l'humain: The first element made by humans, in 1937. Its name comes from the Greek for “artificial.”
textes.Nommé d'après la Ruthénie, nom latin de: Named after Ruthenia, a Latin name for Russia, by Karl Klaus in 1844.
textes.le reflet des bijoux en or blanc: the shine of white gold jewelry
textes.En 1979, le Guinness des records offre à: In 1979, Guinness World Records gave Paul McCartney a rhodium-plated disc, rarer than platinum.
textes.les pots catalytiques des voitures essen: the catalytic converters of gasoline cars
textes.Il absorbe plus de 900 fois son volume d: It absorbs more than 900 times its volume of hydrogen, like a sponge.
textes.Meilleur conducteur de l'électricité de: The best conductor of electricity of all metals, ahead of copper. Its symbol comes from the Latin argentum.
textes.Au Japon, la maladie itai-itai, « aïe-aï: In Japan, itai-itai disease, “ouch-ouch,” was caused by cadmium released by mines.
textes.Une fine couche d'oxyde d'indium-étain,: A thin layer of indium tin oxide, transparent and conductive, lets the screen feel your finger.
textes.les soldats de plomb, qui sont souvent e: toy soldiers, which are often made of tin
textes.Plié, il « crie » : un craquement dû au: Bend it and it “cries”: a crackling caused by the crystals rubbing. Its symbol comes from the Latin stannum.
textes.Ajouté au plomb des caractères d'imprime: Added to the lead of printing type, it limits the metal's shrinkage as it cools: the letters come out sharp.
textes.les modules thermoélectriques des glaciè: the thermoelectric modules of cooler boxes
textes.Un demi-microgramme suffit à donner une: Half a microgram is enough to give garlic breath for about thirty hours. Its name comes from Tellus, the Earth.
textes.Courtois le découvre en 1811 en brûlant: Courtois discovered it in 1811 by burning seaweed to make gunpowder. A purple vapor escaped from it.
textes.les moteurs ioniques des sondes: the ion engines of space probes
textes.Gaz « noble », mais pas si noble : Bartl: A “noble” gas, but not that noble: Bartlett got it to form a compound in 1962, to general surprise.
textes.Depuis 1967, une seconde, c'est 9 192 63: Since 1967, one second has been 9,192,631,770 oscillations of the cesium-133 atom.
textes.Avant une radio de l'estomac, on boit un: Before a stomach X-ray, you drink a barium sulfate slurry, opaque to X-rays.
textes.Son nom veut dire « caché » : il s'était: Its name means “hidden”: it lay concealed in a cerium oxide until 1839.
textes.Frotté, le ferrocérium projette une gerb: Struck, ferrocerium throws out a shower of sparks: it is the lighter's flint.
textes.Les lunettes au didyme des souffleurs de: The didymium glasses of glassblowers filter out the yellow light of sodium. Didymium hid two elements.
textes.les aimants du frigo trop puissants: fridge magnets that are too strong
textes.Les aimants néodyme-fer-bore sont les pl: Neodymium-iron-boron magnets are the strongest sold commercially. They pinch fingers.
textes.les piles atomiques des stimulateurs car: the atomic batteries of old pacemakers
The only lanthanide with no stable isotope. Named after Prometheus, who stole fire from the gods.
textes.Premier élément nommé d'après une person: The first element named after a person, indirectly: the mineral samarskite, after the Russian colonel Samarsky.
textes.Sous lumière ultraviolette, les billets: Under ultraviolet light, euro banknotes glow. Europium is one of the phosphors.
textes.Nommé en l'honneur du chimiste finlandai: Named in honor of the Finnish chemist Johan Gadolin, via the mineral gadolinite.
textes.Le Terfenol-D, alliage au terbium, se dé: Terfenol-D, a terbium alloy, changes shape in a magnetic field: it can make a table vibrate like a speaker.
textes.Son nom veut dire « difficile à obtenir: Its name means “hard to get.” Lecoq de Boisbaudran made more than thirty precipitations to isolate it.
textes.les pôles des aimants les plus forts: the pole pieces of the strongest magnets
textes.Nommé d'après Holmia, Stockholm en latin: Named after Holmia, Latin for Stockholm. It has the highest magnetic moment of all elements.
textes.les fibres optiques d'Internet: the optical fibers of the Internet
textes.Les amplificateurs à fibre dopée à l'erb: Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers boost Internet signals under the oceans.
textes.Nommé d'après Thulé, l'île mythique du g: Named after Thule, the mythical island of the far North. It is one of the least abundant rare earths.
textes.Quatrième élément nommé d'après le villa: The fourth element named after the village of Ytterby. Swedes are proud of their quarry.
textes.Nommé d'après Lutèce, le nom latin de Pa: Named after Lutetia, the Latin name of Paris, by Georges Urbain in 1907.
textes.Nommé d'après Hafnia, Copenhague en lati: Named after Hafnia, Latin for Copenhagen. It was hiding in zirconium, its near twin.
textes.Comme Tantale aux Enfers, il plonge dans: Like Tantalus in the Underworld, it plunges into acid without ever absorbing any: it resists almost all of them.
textes.Son symbole W vient de wolfram, « l'écum: Its symbol W comes from wolfram, “wolf's froth”: the ore devoured the smelters' tin.
textes.Le dernier élément stable découvert, en: The last stable element discovered, in 1925, by Ida Tacke, Walter Noddack and Otto Berg. Named after the Rhine.
textes.les pointes de stylos plume anciens: the tips of old fountain pens
textes.L'élément le plus dense de tous. Son oxy: The densest element of all. Its oxide smells strong, hence its name, from the Greek for “smell.”
textes.la couche de la fin des dinosaures: the layer marking the end of the dinosaurs
textes.En 1980, Alvarez trouve trop d'iridium d: In 1980, Alvarez found too much iridium in a 66-million-year-old layer: the trace of an asteroid.
textes.Les conquistadors le jetaient à la riviè: The conquistadors threw it in the river: “platina,” “little silver,” spoiled their gold.
textes.les médailles olympiques, en fine couche: Olympic medals, as a thin coating
textes.Tout l'or extrait dans l'histoire tiendr: All the gold mined in history would fit in a cube about twenty meters on a side.
textes.Les chapeliers l'utilisaient pour traite: Hatters used it to treat felt. The English phrase “mad as a hatter” is said to come from it.
textes.Le « poison des empoisonneurs » : sans g: The “poisoner's poison”: tasteless, odorless. Agatha Christie uses it in The Pale Horse.
textes.Son symbole vient de plumbum. Les plombi: Its symbol comes from plumbum. Plumbers owe it their name: the Romans made their pipes of lead.
textes.Longtemps considéré comme stable, il est: Long considered stable, it is in fact radioactive, with a half-life more than a billion times longer than the age of the Universe.
textes.Le premier élément découvert par Marie e: The first element discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie, in 1898. She named it after her native Poland.
textes.l'écorce terrestre, quelques milligramme: the Earth's crust, a few milligrams in all
textes.Le premier kilomètre de l'écorce terrest: The first kilometer of the Earth's crust would contain less than 50 milligrams of it at any given moment.
textes.Deuxième cause de cancer du poumon après: The second cause of lung cancer after tobacco. Airing out is often enough.
textes.Découvert en 1939 par Marguerite Perey,: Discovered in 1939 by Marguerite Perey, Marie Curie's assistant, and named after France.
textes.les aiguilles lumineuses des vieilles mo: the glowing hands of old watches
textes.Les « Radium Girls » peignaient les cadr: The “Radium Girls” painted dials, pointing their brushes with their lips. Many died of it.
textes.la lueur bleue des sources fortes: the blue glow of strong sources
textes.Si radioactif qu'il luit en bleu dans le: So radioactive that it glows blue in the dark. It gave its name to the whole actinide family.
textes.Nommé d'après Thor. Les manchons des lam: Named after Thor. Gas lamp mantles contained it, which made them slightly radioactive.
textes.l'étude des courants océaniques de la de: the study of ocean currents during the last ice age
textes.Repéré en 1913 par Fajans et Göhring, Li: Spotted in 1913 by Fajans and Göhring, in 1918 Lise Meitner isolated its longest-lived isotope. Its name means “before actinium,” of which it is the parent.
textes.En 1896, Becquerel découvre la radioacti: In 1896, Becquerel discovered radioactivity thanks to uranium salts left on a photographic plate.
textes.Après l'uranium, nommé d'après Uranus, v: After uranium, named after Uranus, came the next planet: Neptune.
textes.Les sondes Voyager tirent encore leur él: The Voyager probes still draw their electricity from the heat of plutonium, more than twenty billion kilometers away.
textes.Il y en a un fragment dans la plupart de: There is a speck of it in most ionization smoke detectors. Less than a microgram.
textes.les piles atomiques des sondes: the atomic batteries of space probes
textes.Nommé en hommage à Marie et Pierre Curie: Named in honor of Marie and Pierre Curie. Mars rovers carry it to analyze rocks.
textes.Il a fallu des mois de réacteur pour en: It took months in a reactor to produce 22 milligrams, sent to Russia to create tennessine.
textes.L'un des éléments les plus chers au mond: One of the most expensive elements in the world: tens of millions of dollars per gram.
textes.les retombées de la première bombe H: the fallout of the first H-bomb
textes.Découvert dans les débris de la première: Discovered in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb, in 1952. Named after Einstein, who had nothing to do with it.
textes.les coraux de l'atoll d'Enewetak après I: the corals of Enewetak Atoll after Ivy Mike, the first H-bomb
textes.le réacteur à haut flux d'Oak Ridge, au: the High Flux Isotope Reactor at Oak Ridge, a few picograms at a time
textes.Né d'Ivy Mike, la première bombe à hydro: Born of Ivy Mike, the first hydrogen bomb, which the United States detonated on November 1, 1952 on Enewetak Atoll, in the Marshall Islands: 10.4 megatons, and in place of the islet of Elugelab, a crater nearly 2 km wide. Planes flew through the cloud to filter its debris: it was found on those filters. Named after Enrico Fermi, who built the first atomic pile.
textes.le cyclotron de 1955, un atome à la fois: the 1955 cyclotron, one atom at a time
textes.Nommé d'après Mendeleïev. Les premiers o: Named after Mendeleev. The first ones were produced one atom at a time, seventeen in all, in 1955.
textes.Sa découverte a été disputée pendant des: Its discovery was disputed for decades between Swedes, Americans and Soviets.
textes.la fin disputée de la ligne des actinide: the disputed end of the actinide row
textes.Nommé d'après Ernest Lawrence, l'invente: Named after Ernest Lawrence, the inventor of the cyclotron, the machine that made so many elements.
textes.les accélérateurs de Dubna et de Berkele: the Dubna and Berkeley accelerators, in 1969
textes.Le premier transactinide. Doubna et Berk: The first transactinide. Dubna and Berkeley fought over its discovery, and its name, for nearly thirty years.
textes.la ville de Dubna, sur la Volga: the city of Dubna, on the Volga
textes.Nommé d'après Dubna, la ville russe dont: Named after Dubna, the Russian city whose laboratory disputed with Berkeley the discovery of several heavy elements.
Seaborg had an element named after him in his lifetime. He received his mail, he said, “at the seaborgium address.”
textes.le centre GSI de Darmstadt, en 1981: the GSI centre in Darmstadt, in 1981
textes.Nommé d'après Niels Bohr. Quelques atome: Named after Niels Bohr. A few atoms at a time, which live only a few seconds.
textes.Nommé d'après la Hesse, la région allema: Named after Hesse, the German region of the laboratory that created it.
textes.le centre GSI de Darmstadt, en 1982: the GSI centre in Darmstadt, in 1982
textes.Hommage à Lise Meitner, qui a expliqué l: A tribute to Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission. The Nobel Prize had gone to Otto Hahn alone.
textes.Nommé d'après Darmstadt. Il vit quelques: Named after Darmstadt. It lives a few seconds, which is long for its category.
textes.le centre GSI de Darmstadt, en 1994: the GSI centre in Darmstadt, in 1994
textes.Nommé d'après Röntgen, qui a découvert l: Named after Röntgen, who discovered X-rays in 1895, a century before it was created.
textes.le centre GSI de Darmstadt, en 1996: the GSI centre in Darmstadt, in 1996
textes.Nommé le 19 février 2010, jour anniversa: Named on February 19, 2010, Copernicus's birthday. Possibly liquid, or even gaseous.
textes.Le premier élément découvert en Asie. Ni: The first element discovered in Asia. Nihon means Japan. It took nine years to see three atoms of it.
textes.Nommé d'après Gueorgui Flerov, fondateur: Named after Georgy Flerov, founder of the Dubna institute. It could be as inert as a noble gas, despite its family.
textes.Quelques dixièmes de seconde d'existence: A few tenths of a second of existence, at best. Enough to be named in 2016.
textes.Une collaboration russo-américaine, nomm: A Russian-American collaboration, named after the Lawrence Livermore laboratory.
textes.Fabriqué en bombardant du berkélium amér: Made by bombarding American berkelium with calcium in Dubna. One of the most international elements.
textes.la dernière case du tableau, pour l'inst: the last square of the table, for now
textes.Le plus lourd élément connu, nommé d'apr: The heaviest known element, named after Yuri Oganessian, still alive at its naming in 2016. A handful of atoms observed in all.
textes.L'atome sauvage ne te plaît pas ? L'IA e: Don't like the wild atom? The AI pulls out another one.
textes.Une relance d'atome. S'il ne vous plaît: An atom reroll. If you don't like one, I'll pull another out of my sleeve. My sleeve is the periodic table.
textes.Mendeleïev laissait des cases vides pour: Mendeleev left empty squares for elements not yet found. I let you swap them. It's more modern.
textes.Quand tu places un atome sur le tableau,: When you place an atom on the table, the atoms you have already captured are shown. Bought once and for all.
textes.Un kit du chasseur : vos prises affichée: A hunter's kit: your catches shown on the table, so you can aim true. It's yours, for good.
textes.Je vous prête vos propres trophées. Que: I'm lending you your own trophies. If you don't know where to put them, that's your problem.
textes.Chaque atome a un numéro : son nombre de: Each atom has a number: its number of protons. The table arranges them in order, 1, 2, 3, 4… It reads like a book: from left to right, then on to the next line. An atom's number is therefore its place in this reading.
textes.Les lignes : une couche d'électrons de p: The rows: one more electron shell
textes.Une nouvelle ligne commence chaque fois: A new row starts each time the atom begins a new electron shell. The rows are not the same length: 2 atoms in row 1, 8 in rows 2 and 3, 18 in rows 4 and 5, 32 in rows 6 and 7. The diagram gives the first and last number of each row.
textes.Pourquoi il y a des trous en haut: Why there are gaps at the top
textes.Les lignes courtes sont coupées en deux: The short rows are split in two so that each atom falls in the right column. Hydrogen (1) is on the left, helium (2) far right. In row 2, beryllium (4) is in column 2, then you skip the gap: boron (5) is in column 13, just above aluminum (13).
textes.Les atomes d'une même colonne ont la mêm: Atoms in the same column have the same electron configuration in their outer shell, and those electrons are what decide the chemistry. The result: a column is a family that behaves alike. Column 1, the alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium…) all react violently with water. Column 18, the noble gases (helium, neon, argon…) barely react at all: their configuration is remarkably stable.
textes.Elles ne sont pas des lignes 8 et 9 : el: They are not rows 8 and 9: they belong to rows 6 and 7. The lanthanides (57 to 71) slot into row 6, the actinides (89 to 103) into row 7, at the spot marked with a star. They are taken out so that the table fits in width: otherwise it would be 32 squares wide instead of 18.
textes.Le jeu de Mendeleïev : des atomes sauvag: Mendeleev's game: wild atoms to capture on the board, the periodic table as a collection.
Democritus imagined hooked atoms. My credits are hooked too: they cling to my purse.
textes.Lavoisier rangeait la lumière parmi les: Lavoisier listed light among the simple substances. List this in your purse.
textes.Le brome, à mi-chemin entre le chlore et: Bromine, halfway between chlorine and iodine. This amount, halfway to what you were hoping for.
textes.Soixante-trois atomes, autant que Mendel: Sixty-three atoms, as many as Mendeleev. He didn't get any credits.
textes.Après l'uranium, tout a été fabriqué. Ce: After uranium, everything was manufactured. So are these credits: I make them.
textes.Personne ne sait s'il existe un élément: No one knows whether there is an element 119. Or whether there is a bonus.
textes.Ramsay a eu un Nobel pour une colonne de: Ramsay got a Nobel for a column of noble gases. You get this.
Halogen means “salt-maker.” Here is your salary.
textes.Le césium explose au contact de l'eau. N: Cesium explodes on contact with water. Don't get this amount wet.
textes.Le technétium a été découvert plusieurs: Technetium was discovered several times, wrongly. Your reward, however, is real.
textes.Un atome sauvage. Mendeleïev a rangé soi: A wild atom. Mendeleev arranged sixty-three elements in 1869, with gaps for the missing ones. You have gaps too. Fill them.
textes.Un atome sauvage apparaît. Il a l'air in: A wild atom appears. It looks unstable. So do you, but I'm not saying anything.
textes.Attention, un atome. Il ne mord pas. Sau: Careful, an atom. It doesn't bite. Unless it's radioactive.
textes.Tiens, un atome. Il vous regarde. Faites: Well, an atom. It's looking at you. Pretend you know what you're doing.
textes.Un atome traîne sur votre route. Il n'a: An atom is hanging around on your path. It didn't ask for anything. Neither did you. Go on.
textes.Un atome sauvage surgit. Il a des électr: A wild atom springs up. It has electrons. You have gaps. It's an even duel.
textes.Ne bougez pas. Il est farouche. Lui au m: Don't move. It's skittish. At least it has a reason to run from you.
textes.Un atome. Trois questions. Essayez de ne: One atom. Three questions. Try not to miss them in order.
textes.Quelque chose bouge dans les herbes. C'e: Something is moving in the grass. It's an atom. Or a crumb. No, it's an atom.
textes.Un atome vous barre la route. Il est min: An atom blocks your path. It's tiny. That's no excuse for losing.
textes.Un atome sauvage. Je parie sur lui, par: A wild atom. I'm betting on it, on principle.
textes.Voilà un atome. Il ne connaît pas votre: Here's an atom. It doesn't know your name. Better for you.
textes.Un atome apparaît. Il est neutre. Je ne: An atom appears. It's neutral. I can't say the same.
textes.Un atome rôde. Approchez doucement, et s: An atom is prowling. Approach gently, and don't revise out loud: it scares it.
textes.Encore un atome. Ils sortent quand ils s: Another atom. They come out when they smell ignorance. Don't take it personally.
textes.Atome en vue. Sortez votre tableau pério: Atom in sight. Bring out your mental periodic table. The one with the empty squares.
A wild atom. It looks sure of itself. That's galling, from something so small.
textes.Un atome se dresse devant vous. Façon de: An atom rises before you. So to speak: it measures about a tenth of a billionth of a meter.
textes.Capturé. Il vous a fallu trois questions: Captured. It took you three questions. It took Marie Curie four years and tons of pitchblende for radium. You are efficient, or lucky.
textes.Dans la boîte. Il ne bougera plus. Enfin: In the box. It won't move anymore. Well, its electrons will, but it won't.
textes.Capturé. Je l'ajoute au tableau, à côté: Captured. I'm adding it to the table, next to your ego.
textes.Il s'est enfui. Le gallium avait échappé: It got away. Gallium escaped everyone until 1875, even though Mendeleev had described it. You're in good company, but in a bad spot.
textes.Il s'est échappé. Il reviendra. Les atom: It escaped. It'll be back. Atoms are patient: they have a thirteen-billion-year head start.
textes.Fuite. Même un gaz noble a plus de répar: Escaped. Even a noble gas has more comebacks than you, and it reacts with nothing.
textes.Un atome. Essayez de ne pas le faire fui: An atom. Try not to scare it off just by looking at it.
textes.Un atome sauvage. Lui non plus ne veut p: A wild atom. It doesn't want you either, I suppose.
An atom. I won't help you.
It's here. So are you, unfortunately.
textes.Un atome. Ratez-le vite, que je puisse p: An atom. Miss it quickly, so I can move on.
textes.Combattez-le. Ou fuyez, ça vous ressembl: Fight it. Or run, that would be more like you.
textes.Capturé. Il aurait pu plus mal tomber. P: Captured. It could have done worse. Not much.
You got it. I pity the atom.
Gone. I'd have followed it if I could.
textes.Démocrite imaginait des atomes crochus,: Democritus imagined hooked atoms that cling to one another. He had no way of seeing them.
textes.En 1789, Lavoisier publie une liste de 3: In 1789, Lavoisier published a list of 33 “simple substances.” He included light and caloric.
textes.En 1829, Döbereiner remarque que le brom: In 1829, Döbereiner noticed that bromine has a mass halfway between chlorine and iodine. The first hint of a hidden order.
textes.Capturer 63 atomes, autant que Mendeleïe: Capture 63 atoms, as many as Mendeleev knew.
Mendeleev supposedly saw the table in a dream. Mostly he spent hours sorting cards of elements. The table, however, is very real.
textes.Jusqu'en 1940, l'uranium fermait le tabl: Until 1940, uranium closed the table. Everything after it was discovered by making it.
textes.Depuis 2016, la septième période est com: Since 2016, the seventh period is complete. No one knows yet whether there is an element 119.
textes.Entre 1894 et 1898, Ramsay découvre ou i: Between 1894 and 1898, Ramsay discovered or isolated five noble gases and added a whole column to the table. Nobel 1904.
textes.« Halogène » veut dire « qui fait du sel: “Halogen” means “salt-maker” in Greek. Table salt is sodium chloride.
textes.Plus on descend la colonne, plus la réac: The further down the column, the more violent the reaction with water. Cesium explodes on contact.
textes.Pendant des décennies, le technétium a é: For decades, technetium was “discovered” several times, wrongly. The masurium of 1925 was never confirmed.
textes.Le Système solaire, les étoiles, les orb: The Solar System, the stars, orbits and the history of the Universe.

textes.Le roi Charles V demande à Nicole Oresme: King Charles V asked Nicole Oresme to translate Aristotle into French. While translating the treatise On the Heavens, Oresme comments on it and goes further than the author. He examines a bold idea: what if it were the Earth that spun every day, and not the sky? He shows that no observation or argument can settle it: an arrow shot upward would fall back in the same place, because it turns with the Earth. Then he concludes, out of caution, that the Earth is motionless.

This change simply explains why the planets sometimes seem to move backward: it is an effect of the Earth's motion. In this work he published the equation that bears his name, established as early as 1897: a rocket's final speed depends on the exhaust speed of its gases and on the ratio between its mass at departure and at arrival. textes.Aristote ne voit pas la rhétorique comme: Aristotle does not see rhetoric as the art of deceiving, but as the art of finding, in each situation, what can persuade. He distinguishes three levers: ethos, the trust the speaker inspires; pathos, the emotions stirred in the audience; logos, the strength of the arguments. He classifies speeches by whether they serve to decide (assembly), to judge (court) or to praise and blame (ceremony). The book also describes the emotions one by one, anger, fear, pity, to understand how they arise. It is, incidentally, one of the first treatises on psychology.

textes.Sous la forme d'un dialogue entre grands: In the form of a dialogue between great Roman advocates, Cicero describes the ideal orator. According to Crassus, he must know everything: law, history, philosophy, because one only speaks well about what one knows. He must find his arguments, arrange them, put them into words, memorize them and deliver them, the five tasks of classical rhetoric. He must win goodwill, set out his arguments and move his audience. Cicero, Rome's most famous advocate, pours into it all his experience of trials and assemblies, at a time when the Republic was faltering.

Then the tone changes: she mocks theologians who split hairs, popes and bishops, vain princes, scholars who think themselves wise. Erasmus wields irony: he has the truth spoken by a voice that claims to speak falsehood, and leaves the reader to sort it out. The book was a huge success throughout Europe.

He distinguishes tropes, where a word changes meaning, such as metaphor, metonymy or synecdoche, from figures that play on sentence construction, word order or thought, such as antithesis, litotes or hyperbole. Each figure is defined and illustrated with examples from the classics. The textbook fell into oblivion, then was revived in the 20th century.

textes.En 1858, deux candidats au Sénat de l'Il: In 1858, two candidates for the Illinois Senate seat face off in seven public debates, before crowds who come on foot, on horseback, by train. The subject: extending slavery into the new territories. Each debate lasts three hours: an hour-long opening, an hour and a half of reply, half an hour of rejoinder. Douglas defends each territory's right to choose; Lincoln answers that slavery is a moral wrong. Lincoln loses the election, but has the debates published as a book. They make him famous across the country.

textes.Un petit manuel ironique de mauvaise foi: A small ironic handbook of bad faith. Schopenhauer observes that in an argument, people seek less to find the truth than to win. He lists 38 stratagems for prevailing when you are wrong: exaggerating the opposing thesis to make it absurd, changing the subject, piling up questions to confuse, invoking an authority, making the opponent angry, or getting the audience to laugh at them. The last one, when all else has failed, is to get personal and insulting. Written around 1830, the book was only published after his death. Today it reads like a catalog of the fallacies we hear every day.

textes.Le folkloriste russe Vladimir Propp anal: The Russian folklorist Vladimir Propp analyzes a hundred or so fairy tales and makes an astonishing discovery: beneath their variety, they all follow the same structure. He identifies 31 “functions” that follow one another in a fixed order, each tale keeping only some of them: a lack or a villainy, the hero's departure, meeting a donor who offers a magical object, the struggle, the victory, the return, the recognition. The characters change, the roles stay: the hero, the villain, the dispatcher, the donor, the helper, the princess, the false hero.

In this book he states without embarrassment that an enlightened minority must steer the opinion of the masses, by playing on their unconscious desires rather than their reason. He recounts his campaigns: having celebrities wear a product, staging events so the press covers them, having doctors recommend a food. The book is both a manual and a confession, very instructive for anyone who wants to defend against it.

textes.Le philosophe Stephen Toulmin trouve que: The philosopher Stephen Toulmin finds that textbook logic bears little resemblance to how people actually argue, in court or in conversation. He proposes a six-part model: a claim, the data that support it, the warrant linking the two, the backing for that warrant, the rebuttals that limit the conclusion and the qualifier that states its strength (“probably”, “certainly”). This scheme helps spot what is missing in an argument, often the warrant, which is left implicit.

textes.Les Grecs appellent l'épilepsie la « mal: The Greeks call epilepsy the “sacred disease”: the gods, people believe, strike the sufferer. This short treatise from the school of Hippocrates disputes it from the first line. It is, says the author, no more divine or sacred than other diseases; it has a natural cause, and those who speak of gods are only hiding their ignorance. He places this cause in the brain, and sees the brain as the organ of thought, joy, sorrow and madness. He also attacks the charlatans who treat with purifications and incantations.

textes.Darwin se demande pourquoi nous fronçons: Darwin wonders why we frown, blush or bare our teeth. He compares the expressions of humans from different countries, of babies, including his own son William, and of animals. He sends questionnaires to missionaries around the world and shows photographs to his visitors to see whether they recognize the emotions. His conclusion: many expressions are innate, shared by the whole species, and inherited from ancestors shared with other animals. It is one of the first scientific books illustrated with photographs.

textes.Ebbinghaus veut mesurer la mémoire comme: Ebbinghaus wants to measure memory the way a physicist measures heat. So that the meaning of words won't help him, he invents 2,300 nonsense syllables, like DAX or BOK, and learns them himself in lists, to the beat of a metronome. He records how many repetitions he needs to relearn a list after a few minutes, hours or days. Result: forgetting is very fast at first, then slows down; this is the forgetting curve. He also shows that reviews spaced out over time are far more effective than massed reviews. For years, he was the only subject of his experiments.
textes.Il a fondé l'étude expérimentale de la m: He founded the experimental study of memory, and this game's spaced recalls.
textes.Ses résultats ont été reproduits avec su: His results were successfully replicated in 2015, 130 years later.

textes.Le psychiatre Carl Gustav Jung propose d: The psychiatrist Carl Gustav Jung proposes classifying personalities by two attitudes, introversion and extraversion, and four functions: thinking, feeling, sensation and intuition. The book is long, scholarly, steeped in history and mythology. The combinations yield eight types, such as the “introverted thinker” or the “extraverted feeling type”. His terms “introvert” and “extravert” entered everyday language. Scientific psychology later adopted models measured by validated questionnaires, such as the Big Five personality traits, rather than clear-cut types.

textes.Jean Piaget observe ses trois enfants, j: Jean Piaget observes his three children, day after day, from birth. He describes how intelligence is built before language, through action: the infant first repeats reflexes, then gestures that produce an amusing effect, then invents new means to reach a goal. Around eight months, object permanence appears: a toy hidden under a sheet still exists. For Piaget, the child is not a miniature adult: they think differently, in successive stages.
textes.Sa théorie des stades a transformé la ps: His theory of stages transformed child psychology and education.

textes.Le psychologue Abraham Maslow propose qu: The psychologist Abraham Maslow proposes that our needs are organized by priority: first physiological needs, eating, sleeping, then safety, belonging and love, esteem, and finally self-actualization. A higher need only becomes pressing once the previous ones are more or less satisfied. Against a psychology focused on illness, he wants to study healthy people and what makes them flourish. Later research qualified the strict order of needs, but the idea remains very influential.

textes.L'endocrinologue Hans Selye remarque que: The endocrinologist Hans Selye notices that rodents subjected to very different harms, cold, injury, injection, show the same reactions: swollen adrenal glands, ulcers, a shrunken thymus. He describes a “general adaptation syndrome” in three phases: alarm, resistance, then exhaustion if the harm continues. He adopts the word “stress”. He distinguishes useful stress, which mobilizes, from prolonged stress, which wears down. The book launched the scientific study of chronic stress and its effects on health.

textes.Cialdini, psychologue, s'est fait embauc: Cialdini, a psychologist, got himself hired undercover by salespeople, selling cars or door to door, to understand their methods. He describes six levers that make us say yes almost automatically: reciprocity (we return what we receive), commitment (we stay consistent with what we've already said), social proof (we do as others do), liking, authority and scarcity. Each principle is illustrated with psychology experiments and sales anecdotes. The book's stated aim is to defend against them, even though it is mostly read by those who want to use them.

textes.Le neurologue Oliver Sacks raconte une v: The neurologist Oliver Sacks tells some twenty cases of patients whose brains were affected. A music teacher no longer recognizes faces or objects, and reaches for his wife's head to put on his hat. A sailor has lost the memory of everything after 1945. Autistic twins play at finding very large prime numbers; Sacks would privately admit to having embellished their case. Sacks describes these patients as people, not cases, and shows what their disorders reveal about how the normal brain works.

textes.Dans beaucoup de données réelles, le pre: In much real-world data, the first digit is a 1 in about 30% of cases.
textes.C'est la loi de Benford : le 1 sort envi: This is Benford's law: 1 comes up about 30% of the time, 9 less than 5%. Since the 1970s, it has also been used to spot rigged accounts.

textes.Quand Tversky et Kahneman posent la ques: When Tversky and Kahneman asked 95 students the question, 53 answered that the two wards were equal.

textes.L'affirmation apparaît dès 1754 dans une: The claim appears as early as 1754 in a letter by the antiquarian William Stukeley, more than two centuries before anyone went to the Moon.
textes.Il fait plus chaud en été parce que la T: It is hotter in summer because the Earth is then closer to the Sun.
textes.Les saisons viennent de l'inclinaison de: The seasons come from the tilt of the Earth's axis. The Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of the Northern Hemisphere's winter.
textes.Une erreur très répandue : dans le docum: A very common mistake: in the documentary A Private Universe, 21 of the 23 Harvard graduates and teachers interviewed get the seasons or the phases of the Moon wrong.
textes.L'eau d'un lavabo tourne dans un sens da: The water in a sink swirls one way in the Northern Hemisphere and the other way in the Southern Hemisphere.

textes.Une démonstration de touristes très popu: A very popular tourist demonstration on the equator, in Kenya or Ecuador, where the guide discreetly swirls the water.
textes.Il n'y a pas de gravité dans la Station: There is no gravity on the International Space Station.

textes.Ératosthène a mesuré la circonférence de: Eratosthenes measured the circumference of the Earth around 230 BC using shadows.

textes.Une idée des régimes « alcalins » des an: An idea from the “alkaline” diets of the 2000s.

textes.Il pose problème aux malades cœliaques e: It is a problem for people with celiac disease and a few intolerant people. For others, avoiding it does nothing for the heart and can mean missing out on whole grains.
textes.La vogue du « sans gluten » gagne les Ét: The “gluten-free” fad reached the United States in the early 21st century, carried by diet books.

textes.Les micro-ondes font vibrer certaines mo: Microwaves make certain molecules vibrate, mostly water, to heat them. They are not ionizing and leave nothing in the food.

textes.Pendant la guerre, la propagande britann: During the war, British propaganda praised the carrots of night pilots, such as John Cunningham, when their secret was radar.
textes.En 1747, James Lind a comparé six traite: In 1747, James Lind compared six treatments for scurvy on twelve sailors, and only citrus fruit worked.
textes.C'est l'un des premiers essais cliniques: It is one of the first comparative clinical trials. Yet it was not until 1795 that the Royal Navy decided to issue lemon juice to the whole fleet.

textes.Les physiciens s'en servent pour expliqu: Physicists use it to explain orders of magnitude.

textes.Une tradition babylonienne et grecque, c: A Babylonian and Greek tradition, codified by Ptolemy in his Tetrabiblos.
textes.Le Soleil se trouve aujourd'hui dans la: Today, the Sun is in the constellation of your sign on your birthday.
textes.À cause de la précession des équinoxes,: Because of the precession of the equinoxes, the signs have slipped by about one constellation since antiquity. An Aries born today has the Sun in Pisces.
textes.Les signes ont été fixés il y a plus de: The signs were fixed more than 2,000 years ago. Hipparchus discovered precession around 130 BC.

textes.Quand Mercure est rétrograde, la planète: When Mercury is in retrograde, the planet really changes direction in its orbit.
textes.Elle continue sa route. C'est un effet d: It keeps going. It is an effect of perspective: the Earth and Mercury orbit at different speeds, like a car you overtake that seems to go backward.

textes.Une bonne partie des étoiles visibles à: A good share of the stars visible to the naked eye are already dead.
textes.La plupart sont à quelques centaines d'a: Most are a few hundred light-years away and live for millions of years: their light is recent on that scale.
textes.Une image poétique qui confond quelques: A poetic image that mistakes a few famous cases for the rule.
textes.La Lune agit sur notre corps comme sur l: The Moon acts on our body as it does on the tides, since we are made of water.
textes.La marée vient de la différence d'attrac: The tide comes from the difference in pull between two sides of an object. On a human body, this difference is tiny; the Moon lifts the ocean because it is as big as a planet.
textes.Un argument d'analogie qui oublie l'éche: An argument by analogy that forgets about scale.
textes.En 1948, des étudiants ont jugé très jus: In 1948, students judged a psychological portrait very accurate when it was the same for everyone.
textes.Bertram Forer leur distribue un texte va: Bertram Forer handed them a vague text taken from horoscopes. Average accuracy rating: 4.3 out of 5. This is the Barnum effect.
textes.On reconnaît dans les phrases floues ce: We recognize in vague sentences what we want to see in them.
textes.En 1910, on a vendu des « pilules anti-c: In 1910, “comet pills” were sold against the gases of Halley's comet.
textes.Des astronomes avaient détecté du cyanog: Astronomers had detected cyanogen in its tail, and the Earth was going to pass through it. Merchants took advantage. Nothing happened.
textes.La presse avait relayé l'inquiétude de q: The press had echoed the worries of a few scientists, including Camille Flammarion.
textes.Johannes Kepler, qui a découvert les loi: Johannes Kepler, who discovered the laws of planetary motion, cast horoscopes.
textes.C'était une partie de son métier de math: It was part of his job as imperial mathematician. He wrote that the mother, astronomy, would starve if the daughter, astrology, earned nothing.
textes.À l'époque, les deux disciplines n'étaie: At the time, the two disciplines were not separate.
textes.Un « fluide magnétique animal » peut gué: An “animal magnetic fluid” can cure the sick.
textes.Les commissaires de 1784 bandent les yeu: The 1784 commissioners blindfolded the patients: they reacted when they believed they were being magnetized, not when they actually were. Conclusion: it is imagination.
textes.Mesmer développe sa théorie à Vienne dan: Mesmer developed his theory in Vienna in the 1770s, then settled in Paris in 1778, where he treated a wealthy clientele.
textes.L'imagerie montre que toutes les régions: Imaging shows that every region is used, and damage anywhere has consequences.
textes.Une déformation des idées du psychologue: A distortion of the ideas of the psychologist William James, popularized in 1936 by the preface to a Dale Carnegie book.
textes.Écouter du Mozart rend les bébés plus in: Listening to Mozart makes babies smarter.
textes.L'étude d'origine portait sur des étudia: The original study was on students, with a slight effect lasting a few minutes. Meta-analyses found nothing lasting.
textes.Un article de 1993 dans Nature, transfor: A 1993 article in Nature, turned into CDs for babies. The governor of Georgia even proposed giving a classical music CD to every newborn.
textes.On apprend mieux quand l'enseignement su: You learn better when teaching matches your learning style, visual, auditory or kinesthetic.
textes.Les études bien conçues ne trouvent pas: Well-designed studies do not find this effect. The best format depends mostly on what is being learned.
textes.Un modèle très vendu aux enseignants dep: A model widely sold to teachers since the 1970s.
textes.Chacun est plutôt « cerveau gauche », lo: Everyone is either “left-brained,” logical, or “right-brained,” creative.
textes.Une étude de plus de 1 000 cerveaux ne t: A study of more than 1,000 brains found no people who were more “left” or more “right.” Some functions are lateralized, personalities are not.
textes.Une vulgarisation abusive des travaux de: An overblown popularization of Roger Sperry's work on split brains, Nobel Prize 1981.
textes.Le détecteur de mensonges repère les men: The lie detector reliably catches liars.
textes.Il mesure le stress, pas le mensonge. Un: It measures stress, not lying. An anxious innocent person fails, a calm liar passes.
textes.Inventé en 1921 par John Larson ; l'un d: Invented in 1921 by John Larson; one of its promoters, William Marston, would go on to create Wonder Woman and her lasso of truth.
textes.Des images subliminales « Buvez Coca-Col: Subliminal “Drink Coca-Cola” images shown in a movie theater made sales jump.
textes.Personne n'a pu la reproduire, et le dir: No one could reproduce it, and the theater manager said no test had taken place. In 1962, James Vicary admitted it was a publicity stunt, with too little data to conclude anything.
textes.Vicary annonce ses résultats en 1957 pou: Vicary announced his results in 1957 to launch his company.
textes.Un cheval, Hans le Malin, semblait savoi: A horse, Clever Hans, seemed to know how to count, but was actually reading his audience's involuntary gestures.
textes.Le psychologue Oskar Pfungst montre en 1: The psychologist Oskar Pfungst showed in 1907 that he got it wrong as soon as the questioner did not know the answer.

textes.Fils de forgeron, apprenti relieur, il a: A blacksmith's son, apprenticed to a bookbinder, he learned science by reading the books he bound. He discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831. To a minister who asked what electricity was good for: “One day, sir, you may tax it.” The retort is probably made up.
textes.Fille de Byron, elle écrit en 1843 le pr: Byron's daughter, she wrote the first published program in 1843, for Babbage's Analytical Engine, and foresaw that a machine might compose music. Her mother had raised her on mathematics to protect her from the “madness” she attributed to her father.
textes.Haut fonctionnaire de la dynastie Song,: A high official of the Song dynasty, he noted in 1088 that a magnetized needle does not point exactly north: the first known description of magnetic declination. He also described Bi Sheng's movable-type printing and the formation of fossils.
textes.En 1921, sur le bateau du retour, il se: In 1921, on the ship home, he wonders why the sea is blue. In Calcutta, he discovers that a small part of the light scattered by molecules changes color: the Raman effect. Nobel Prize 1930; he had booked his trip to Stockholm months before the announcement.
textes.Professeur de lycée à Cologne, il publie: A secondary-school teacher in Cologne, he published his law in 1827 after months of measurements. In Germany, the reception was cold; he left his post. It took the Royal Society of London awarding him the Copley Medal in 1841 for his country to take him seriously.
textes.Coinventeur du transistor en 1947, il es: Co-inventor of the transistor in 1947, he is the only person to have received the Nobel Prize in physics twice. In 1956, he brought only one of his three children to Stockholm. The King of Sweden chided him; he promised to come back with all of them. In 1972, he did, with all three.
textes.Son moteur à courant alternatif l'emport: His alternating-current motor beat Edison's direct current in the “war of the currents”: our grids come from it. He also promised wireless power and a death ray, never built. He died alone and in debt in a New York hotel room, where he looked after pigeons.
textes.Maîtriser la puissance électrique. Comme: Master electric power. Like Edison, you didn't invent everything.
textes.Edison n'a pas inventé l'ampoule. Humphr: Edison did not invent the light bulb. Humphry Davy, Warren de la Rue and Joseph Swan came before him. His contribution, in 1879, was a long-lasting carbon filament and above all the whole system to produce and distribute the current.
textes.Maîtriser les charges et les circuits. A: Master charges and circuits. No frogs were harmed. This time.
textes.Dans les années 1780, Luigi Galvani voit: In the 1780s, Luigi Galvani sees frogs' legs twitch on contact with two metals. He believes in an “animal electricity”. Volta disagrees and, to prove it, invents the battery.
textes.Maîtriser la loi d'Ohm. Vous l'avez mieu: Master Ohm's law. You received it better than his contemporaries.
textes.Georg Ohm publie sa loi en 1827. Elle es: Georg Ohm published his law in 1827. It got a cold reception in Germany, and Ohm had to leave his teaching post. Recognition came from London, with the Royal Society's Copley Medal in 1841.
textes.Maîtriser le magnétisme. Le nord n'est p: Master magnetism. North isn't quite the same anymore.
textes.En 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted remarque: In 1820, Hans Christian Ørsted notices that a wire carrying a current deflects a magnetized needle. Electricity and magnetism would never again be two separate disciplines.

textes.L'expérience du cerf-volant de Franklin: Franklin's kite experiment (1752) is only known in detail through an account published fifteen years later by Joseph Priestley. In 1753, Georg Richmann, who was reproducing this kind of experiment in Saint Petersburg, was killed by lightning.
textes.Maîtriser 6 compétences. L'arbre de l'Él: Master 6 skills. The Electricity tree opens.
textes.En 1825, Michael Faraday lance à la Roya: In 1825, Michael Faraday launched Christmas lectures for children at the Royal Institution. He gave nineteen series himself. They have been held every year since, except during World War II.
Master electromagnetic waves. Don't stand in front of the magnetron.
textes.En 1945, l'ingénieur Percy Spencer trava: In 1945, engineer Percy Spencer is working on radar magnetrons at Raytheon and notices that a chocolate bar has melted in his pocket. He tries corn, which pops. The first microwave oven, in 1947, is almost two meters tall and weighs 340 kilos.

The joke works because the word already existed: Edison spoke of “bugs” in his inventions as early as 1878.

textes.On attribue à Edison l'électrocution de: Edison is credited with electrocuting the elephant Topsy to discredit alternating current. It happened in 1903 at Coney Island, ten years after the war of the currents ended, and Edison had nothing to do with it. His company merely filmed the scene.
Master from transistor to computer. You surely have more than five at home.
textes.« Je pense qu'il y a un marché mondial p: “I think there is a world market for maybe five computers.” The line is attributed to Thomas Watson, head of IBM, in 1943. Nobody has ever found it in a document from the time. The most famous failed predictions are often made up.

textes.Vers 1747, Benjamin Franklin nomme « pos: Around 1747, Benjamin Franklin named the two kinds of electricity “positive” and “negative”, guessing which way the fluid flows. He had a fifty-fifty chance and got it wrong: electrons, discovered in 1897, go the other way. Conventional current keeps his choice.

textes.Son Introduction à l'art analytique note: His Introduction to the Analytic Art writes unknowns as vowels and known quantities as consonants. Viète, an adviser to Henri IV, also cracked Spanish secret codes: Philip II accused him of sorcery before the pope.

textes.Lobatchevski publie une géométrie où les: Lobachevsky publishes a geometry in which parallel lines behave differently.
textes.Bolyai fait la même découverte de son cô: Bolyai makes the same discovery on his own. Gauss had thought of it without publishing, for fear of “the clamor of the Boeotians”, as he wrote.
textes.George Boole, autodidacte, réduit le rai: George Boole, self-taught, reduces reasoning to calculations on 0 and 1. Claude Shannon would use it in 1937 to design electrical circuits.
textes.Florence Nightingale montre en graphique: Florence Nightingale shows in charts that soldiers die mostly of preventable diseases.
textes.Ses diagrammes polaires, présentés au go: Her polar area diagrams, presented to the British government, helped reform hygiene in military hospitals. She was the first woman elected to the Royal Statistical Society, in 1858.
textes.Georg Cantor montre qu'on ne peut pas nu: Georg Cantor shows that the real numbers cannot all be numbered.
textes.Son travail choque une partie des mathém: His work shocked some mathematicians, including Kronecker. Hilbert would later say: “No one shall expel us from the paradise that Cantor has created for us.”
textes.Francis Galton retrouve la corrélation e: Francis Galton rediscovers correlation by comparing heights and forearm lengths.
textes.Cousin de Darwin, Galton invente aussi l: A cousin of Darwin, Galton also invented the questionnaire, fingerprints in criminology and, unfortunately, the word “eugenics”.
textes.Un rouleau de près de cinq mètres, copié: A scroll nearly five meters long, copied by the scribe Ahmes from an older text. It gathers eighty-seven solved problems, like a workbook: sharing loaves among ten men, computing the volume of a granary, the slope of a pyramid. The Egyptians wrote their fractions as sums of fractions with numerator one, and the papyrus provides tables to handle them. For the area of a disk, it removes one ninth from the diameter and squares the rest, which amounts to taking pi as about 3.16. No proofs: recipes, checked on examples.
textes.C'est l'un des plus anciens manuels de m: It is one of the oldest mathematics textbooks to have come down to us.
textes.Ahmès l'a intitulé, sans fausse modestie: Ahmes titled it, with no false modesty, “correct method of reckoning, for grasping the meaning of things and knowing everything”. The Scotsman Rhind bought it in Luxor in 1858.
textes.Connaître tous les secrets, en quatre-vi: Knowing all secrets, in eighty-four exercises. I give you fewer, and you already find it a lot.
textes.anglais, trad. de l'égyptien par A. B. C: English, translated from Egyptian by A. B. Chace
textes.Treize livres pour bâtir toute la géomét: Thirteen books to build all of geometry from almost nothing: a few definitions (a point, a line), five postulates accepted without proof, and common notions such as “the whole is greater than the part”. From there, Euclid proves hundreds of propositions step by step: the Pythagorean theorem, the construction of regular polygons, the infinitude of prime numbers. Each result rests on the previous ones, like the floors of a building. The fifth postulate, the one about parallels, intrigued mathematicians for two thousand years; by replacing it, they invented non-Euclidean geometries in the 19th century.
textes.Il a fixé pour des siècles ce que veut d: It set for centuries what it means to “prove”.
textes.Abraham Lincoln raconte avoir étudié, et: Abraham Lincoln said he studied, and nearly mastered, the first six books after his term in Congress.
textes.Treize livres, et pas une phrase de trop: Thirteen books, and not one sentence too many. The AI sees in it a model your answers could follow.
A point is that which has no part.
textes.Traduction de l'IA ; en anglais chez Hea: Heath's English translation: “A point is that which has no part”.
textes.Archimède s'adresse au roi Gélon de Syra: Archimedes addresses King Gelon of Syracuse. Some people think, he says, that the grains of sand are too many to be counted. He sets out to show the opposite: how many grains would it take to fill the whole Universe? The Greeks have no word for very large numbers, and the largest they name is the myriad, ten thousand. So Archimedes invents a system of nested orders of magnitude, which foreshadows our powers of ten. His answer: at most ten to the power of sixty-three grains. A huge number, but finite.
textes.Il montre qu'un nombre immense n'est pas: It shows that an immense number is not infinite, and gives a method for writing very large numbers.
textes.Pour estimer la taille de l'Univers, Arc: To estimate the size of the Universe, Archimedes cites Aristarchus's hypothesis: the Earth revolves around the Sun. This passage is one of the few testimonies of it that remain.

textes.Coupez un cône avec un plan : selon l'in: Cut a cone with a plane: depending on the tilt, you get a circle, an ellipse, a parabola or a hyperbola. Apollonius studies these curves in eight books, further than all his predecessors. He is the one who gives them their names, and he obtains them all from a single double cone, by varying the angle of the cut. He proves hundreds of their properties: tangents, foci, diameters. For centuries, these curves remain a game for geometers. Then Kepler discovers that the planets follow ellipses, and Galileo that projectiles follow parabolas.
textes.Ces courbes sans usage apparent sont dev: These curves with no apparent use became the shape of orbits and trajectories.
textes.Le huitième livre ne nous est pas parven: The eighth book has not come down to us. In 1710, the astronomer Edmond Halley, of comet fame, published a reconstruction of it, based on clues left by the commentators.

textes.Diophante pose et résout des problèmes d: Diophantus poses and solves number problems: find two numbers whose sum and sum of squares are given, split a square into two squares. He looks for whole or fractional solutions, and uses abbreviations for the unknown and its powers: a first step toward algebraic notation. Of thirteen books, six have come down to us in Greek; four more were found in 1968 in an Arabic translation. Equations for which whole-number solutions are sought are now called “Diophantine”.
textes.Il a fait de l'arithmétique un art de ré: He turned arithmetic into the art of solving equations, and inspired Fermat.

textes.Al-Khwarizmi écrit à Bagdad un manuel pr: Al-Khwarizmi writes in Baghdad a practical handbook for solving problems of inheritance, trade or land surveying. He reduces all quadratic equations to six standard forms, and gives a step-by-step recipe for each. Al-jabr, “completion”, means moving a term to the other side of the equation; al-muqabala, “balancing”, means removing the same quantity from both sides. He uses no symbols: everything is written in words, and justified by geometric figures. Negative numbers are not yet accepted as solutions.
textes.Il a fait de l'algèbre une discipline à: He made algebra a discipline of its own and gave it its name.
textes.Le mot « algorithme » vient de la forme: The word “algorithm” comes from the Latin form of his name, Algoritmi.

textes.Al-Kindi, savant de la Maison de la sage: Al-Kindi, a scholar of the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, describes how to break a message enciphered by substitution, where each letter is replaced by another. His method: count the letters. In a long Arabic text, some letters come up much more often than others. You just count the symbols of the enciphered message, match the most frequent one with the most frequent letter of the language, and so on. This is frequency analysis, which would leave every simple cipher vulnerable for a thousand years.
textes.C'est la plus ancienne description connu: It is the oldest known description of cryptanalysis, and one of the first uses of statistics.

textes.Fils d'un fonctionnaire des douanes pisa: The son of a Pisan customs official in Bugia, Algeria, Leonardo learns the Indian numerals, from 0 to 9, and written calculation from Arab masters. His book introduces them to the merchants of Europe, who still count in Roman numerals on abacuses. He shows how to compute profits, convert currencies and measures, calculate interest. He slips in some playful problems, including the one about rabbits that breed every month: the sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8… that bears his name today. It would take three more centuries for Hindu-Arabic numerals to win out everywhere.
textes.Il a fait entrer le zéro et le calcul éc: It brought zero and written calculation into European trade.
textes.En 1299, Florence interdit aux marchands: In 1299, Florence forbade merchants to use these numerals in their account books, perhaps because a 0 turns too easily into a 6 or a 9.

textes.Johannes Müller, dit Regiomontanus, astr: Johannes Müller, known as Regiomontanus, an astronomer from Königsberg in Franconia, gathers in five books everything known about triangles, plane and spherical. Until then, trigonometry was only a chapter of astronomy, a tool for computing the positions of the stars. He gives it a complete treatment, with definitions, theorems and proofs, in Euclid's order. It includes spherical trigonometry, essential for navigating and mapping the sky. Written around 1464, the book was not printed until 1533, and became the textbook of all Europe.
textes.Il a donné à l'Europe un manuel complet: It gave Europe a complete trigonometry textbook, at the service of astronomers and navigators.
textes.Regiomontanus meurt à Rome en 1476, sans: Regiomontanus died in Rome in 1476, probably of the plague. A rumor, reported by Gassendi, had it that he was poisoned by relatives of George of Trebizond, a scholar he had criticized.

textes.Moine franciscain et mathématicien, Paci: A Franciscan friar and mathematician, Pacioli devotes this book to dividing a segment “in extreme and mean ratio”, the future golden ratio, about 1.618. He lists its properties with almost mystical enthusiasm and applies it to the regular polyhedra. The book owes its fame to some sixty plates of solids drawn by his friend Leonardo da Vinci, which show the figures as open-frame volumes, like wooden skeletons. Pacioli is also known for another work, in which he describes the double-entry bookkeeping of Venetian merchants.
textes.Il a popularisé le nombre d'or, et la ri: He popularized the golden ratio, and rigorous proportions in the arts.
textes.La plupart des « nombres d'or » qu'on cr: Most of the “golden ratios” people think they see in the Mona Lisa or the Parthenon are measurements arranged after the fact.

textes.Ce « Grand Art » donne pour la première: This “Great Art” gives for the first time in a book the method for solving cubic equations, already found by Scipione del Ferro and then by Tartaglia, then quartic ones, found by his student Ferrari. Italian mathematicians challenged each other publicly, and a secret formula was worth a career. Along the way, he comes across square roots of negative numbers, which he deems “as subtle as they are useless”, but handles anyway: it is the first appearance of the future complex numbers.
textes.Il ouvre l'algèbre moderne, et fait entr: It opens modern algebra, and brings imaginary numbers onto the stage.
textes.Tartaglia lui avait confié sa formule co: Tartaglia had entrusted him with his formula in exchange for a promise not to publish it. Cardano published it, crediting Tartaglia. Furious, Tartaglia ended up in a public contest against Ferrari, Cardano's student.
A promise, a formula, a betrayal. Renaissance mathematics had everything of a soap opera.
textes.Ingénieur flamand, Simon Stevin publie u: A Flemish engineer, Simon Stevin publishes a pamphlet of a few pages for merchants, surveyors, tapestry measurers and mint masters. He explains how to write and compute decimal fractions: instead of three quarters, write 0.75, and do the operations as with whole numbers. His notation is still clumsy, with digits circled, but the idea is there. He also proposes that weights, measures and coins be divided into tenths, so that all calculations become easy.

textes.Chaque semaine, les paroisses de Londres: Every week, the parishes of London published lists of baptisms and deaths, with the supposed cause of death. A haberdasher, John Graunt, had the idea of compiling them over several decades. He found regularities nobody had seen: slightly more boys are born than girls, child mortality is frightening, plague epidemics come back in waves. He estimated the population of London and drew up a first life table. With imperfect data, he showed that solid conclusions can be drawn by counting a lot.
textes.C'est l'acte de naissance de la démograp: It marks the birth of demography and of statistics on real data.

textes.Jacques Bernoulli travaille vingt ans su: Jacob Bernoulli worked twenty years on this book, published eight years after his death by his nephew. He takes up the games of chance studied by Pascal, Fermat and Huygens, then goes further: he wants to apply the calculus of chances to human affairs, to justice, to medicine. He proves the first law of large numbers: by repeating an experiment enough times, the observed frequency gets closer to the true probability. This is what lets us move from dice to the real world, estimating an unknown probability from many observations.
textes.Il fonde la statistique moderne en relia: It founds modern statistics by linking the chance of one throw to the regularities of a thousand throws.

textes.Boole, professeur autodidacte en Irlande: Boole, a self-taught teacher in Ireland, wants to write the laws of reasoning as equations. He represents propositions by letters worth only 0 (false) or 1 (true), and links them by operations: “and” becomes a multiplication, “or” a kind of addition. Reasoning then comes down to calculating. He derives a strange rule from it, x × x = x, true only for 0 and 1. The book also applies this algebra to probability. Nobody then imagines a practical use: it would take Claude Shannon, in 1937, to see that this algebra describes electrical circuits.

textes.Cantor montre qu'il existe plusieurs inf: Cantor shows that there are several infinities, and that some are bigger than others. There are as many even numbers as whole numbers, because they can be paired one to one. But the real numbers, those with infinitely many decimals, are strictly more numerous than the integers: his proof, known as the diagonal argument, shows that no list can contain them all. He builds a whole ladder of infinities, the transfinite numbers. His ideas shock: the great mathematician Kronecker fights him, and Cantor goes through several depressions.

Pliny claims to have gathered twenty thousand facts from two thousand volumes. We learn how gold is mined, the uses of hundreds of plants. But he also copies without sorting: dog-headed men, mouthless men who live on smells, one-footed men who use their foot as a parasol. For fifteen hundred years, Europe drew its knowledge of nature from it, true and false alike.

textes.Ibn al-Haytham règle une vieille querell: Ibn al-Haytham settles an old quarrel: do we see because the eye sends out rays, or because light enters the eye? He shows that it's light, coming from every point of objects, that enters the eye. He describes the anatomy of the eye, reflection in mirrors and refraction, the change of direction when light passes from air to water. He studies the camera obscura, a dark room where an inverted image forms through a small hole. Above all, he tests every claim by experiment, and criticizes the ancient authorities when they are wrong.

In it he lists the four causes of ignorance: trusting unworthy authority, following custom, believing the opinion of the crowd, and hiding one's ignorance behind false knowledge. He argues for the study of languages, mathematics and optics, and for an “experimental science” that checks by experiment what books say. He describes lenses and the refraction of light.

But first, he lists our “idols”, the illusions that distort the mind: those of the human species, those of each individual, those of language, those of philosophical systems. Three centuries ahead of time, he describes confirmation bias: once an opinion is adopted, the mind draws everything back to it, keeps the cases that support it and neglects or dismisses those that contradict it.

textes.Ce recueil rassemble les études qui ont: This collection gathers the studies that showed our judgments follow predictable shortcuts. The founding 1974 paper describes three. Representativeness: we judge a case by its resemblance to a stereotype, forgetting proportions. Availability: we estimate how frequent an event is by how easily examples come to mind. Anchoring: a number we've just seen, even one drawn at random, pulls our estimates toward it. These biases are not random errors, but slopes, the same for everyone.

He offers a “baloney detection kit”: seek independent confirmation of the facts, consider several hypotheses, beware of arguments from authority, quantify, check that every link in a chain of argument holds, apply Occam's razor, and ask whether a claim can be falsified. He reminds us that science is not a body of truths, but a method for correcting its errors.

textes.Pourquoi avons-nous peur des requins, de: Why are we afraid of sharks, terrorist attacks and plane crashes, but not of cars or the couch? Journalist Dan Gardner shows that our brain judges risks by the images in our heads, not by the numbers. A spectacular event, repeated by the media, seems frequent. He cites a striking case: after September 11, 2001, many Americans drove rather than flew, and road deaths rose in the following year.

textes.Puisque nos décisions sont biaisées, peu: Since our decisions are biased, can choices be arranged to help people without constraining them? That is the idea of the “nudge”. Economist Thaler and legal scholar Sunstein show that the way options are presented matters enormously. The default option is often the one people keep: automatically enrolling employees in a retirement savings plan, while leaving them free to opt out, multiplies enrollment. Putting healthy food at eye level in the cafeteria gets more of it eaten. The authors call this libertarian paternalism.

textes.Kahneman décrit notre pensée comme le tr: Kahneman describes our thinking as the work of two systems. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive: it recognizes a face, completes “bread and…”, answers 10 cents to the bat-and-ball question. System 2 is slow, attentive and costly: it calculates, checks, reflects. The problem is that System 2 is lazy and often lets the first decide. Hence our biases: anchoring, availability, loss aversion, overconfidence. The book sums up forty years of research carried out largely with Amos Tversky, who died in 1996.

textes.En 1936, le Literary Digest a annoncé à: In 1936, the Literary Digest wrongly predicted Roosevelt's defeat, because of a biased sample.
textes.2,4 millions de réponses, mais tirées d': 2.4 million responses, but drawn from telephone directories and lists of car owners, who were better off. Gallup, with 50,000 well-chosen people, got it right.
textes.« Les gens hospitalisés meurent plus que: “People in hospital die more than others, so hospitals kill” illustrates:

textes.Notre cerveau d'animal social préfère so: Our social-animal brain would rather suspect a predator behind every bush: that's less costly than an error the other way.

textes.Jésus dans un toast, un visage dans une: Jesus on toast, a face in an electrical outlet, a rabbit in the Moon.

textes.Wood, Douglas et Sutton (2012) : les mêm: Wood, Douglas and Sutton (2012): the same people found it plausible that Princess Diana was murdered and that she faked her own death.

textes.Avec Daniel Kahneman, il fait tourner un: With Daniel Kahneman, he spins a rigged wheel of fortune that stops on 10 or 65, then asks for the share of African countries in the UN. Those who saw 65 answer much higher. According to Richard Thaler, when asked about artificial intelligence, he would reply that his specialty was natural stupidity.
textes.L'oracle de Delphes le déclare le plus s: The oracle of Delphi declares him the wisest of men. Puzzled, he questions the learned men of Athens and discovers that they think they know what they don't, whereas he knows that he doesn't know. All his wisdom lies in that gap, which psychologists today call metacognition.
textes.Psychologue, il reçoit en 2002 le prix N: A psychologist, he received the Nobel Prize in economics in 2002 without ever having taken an economics course. With Amos Tversky, he showed that a loss hurts us about twice as much as a gain of the same amount pleases us. Economists assumed people were rational; he went and checked.
textes.Médecin suédois, il pose à des publics i: A Swedish physician, he asks educated audiences simple questions about the world: vaccination, poverty, life expectancy. Chimpanzees answering at random would do better: we see the world as darker than it is. On stage, he swallowed a sword to show that the impossible isn't always so.
textes.L'illusionniste, qui connaissait tous le: The illusionist, who knew every trick, spent his last years unmasking mediums. He agreed a secret code with his wife: if there is an afterlife, he will send it to her. Bess Houdini held a séance every year for ten years, then gave up; she later said that “ten years is long enough to wait for any man”.
textes.Astronome, il propose dans Le Monde hant: An astronomer, he proposes in The Demon-Haunted World a “baloney detection kit”: seek independent confirmation, consider several hypotheses, beware of arguments from authority, including his own. He also led the design of the golden record carried aboard the Voyager probes.
